BUSINESS INFORMATION
Read how enquiries, payments and agreed sales work, and which individual terms must be confirmed before you pay for a bird.
Last updated: 2 October 2026

Crownwing Parrots is a sole-trader parrot breeder and retailer. This website supports enquiries; it does not have an online checkout or take payments through its forms. A downloaded enquiry is not an order, payment or confirmed reservation.

This policy should be read with the quotation, invoice, individual sales agreement and relevant species documentation. Individual terms must be clear before payment and supplied in a form the customer can keep. Nothing in this policy or an individual agreement excludes statutory rights that cannot lawfully be excluded.

Bank transfer is the confirmed payment method. Payment instructions will be provided with the relevant invoice or payment request. Card payments and other methods have not been confirmed and are not advertised as available.

The price of the actual bird, applicable taxes and any agreed extra charges must be disclosed before payment is required. Where transport, documentation, veterinary work or another additional charge applies, its amount or basis must be explained in the quotation or agreement. A species photograph is not a priced offer for that individual bird.

If a deposit is required, its amount, payment deadline, reservation period and treatment on cancellation must be stated in writing before you pay. There is no published standard deposit amount or blanket non-refundable deposit rule.

Unless agreed otherwise in writing, a reservation is confirmed only after the required payment has been received and confirmed by Crownwing Parrots. Do not assume that preparing an enquiry reserves a bird. Any deposit term remains subject to applicable consumer law and must not remove a refund right provided by law.

Collection, UK delivery or delivery to an international destination must be discussed for the specific bird and destination. No standard UK coverage area or international destination list has been confirmed. A city guide is not a promise of a branch, collection point or delivery route.

A proposed handover depends on suitable welfare and transport arrangements, species restrictions, documentation, permits, veterinary requirements and any applicable import or export rules. Delivery may be declined where those requirements cannot be met. Do not travel to the contact address or arrange transport without agreeing the appointment and handover details first.

There is no published flat delivery charge or guaranteed dispatch timeframe. The proposed destination, transport method and relevant additional costs must be confirmed before the customer commits to the arrangement. No additional charge should be imposed without prior disclosure and agreement where required.

Estimated dates are agreed after the bird, documentation and transport arrangements have been confirmed. Weather, carrier availability, veterinary requirements and regulatory procedures can affect the plan. Significant delays should be communicated with an updated proposal; a delay does not remove any applicable statutory delivery or cancellation remedy.

To cancel, email either published business address with your name, bird description and order or invoice reference, if one has been issued. State clearly that you wish to cancel. You do not need to prepare a downloadable website enquiry to make that request.

Cancellation and deposit treatment depend on the applicable law and the terms provided before the sale. Qualifying distance sales can carry a 14-day cancellation right, subject to the applicable rules and lawful exceptions. This website does not assert that every live-bird purchase is exempt, or that every purchase carries an unconditional change-of-mind return right.

No standard voluntary cancellation fee or deposit-forfeiture rule has been decided. Any proposed fee or deposit condition must be explained before payment and must be lawful. An individual agreement cannot override mandatory consumer protections.

Contact Crownwing Parrots before attempting a return so that suitable care, documentation and transport can be coordinated. Do not post, ship or bring a bird to the business address without agreed safe arrangements. Do not delay necessary veterinary care while waiting for a response.

There is no confirmed additional voluntary return window or flat return-transport charge. Any voluntary return arrangement must be agreed in writing. Where a legal right to return or another remedy applies, it takes precedence over discretionary terms; contacting us to coordinate welfare arrangements does not make a statutory right dependent on our approval.

Refunds that are legally due must be made within the applicable statutory deadline. For qualifying distance-sale cancellations, the reimbursement rules can depend on receipt of returned goods or evidence of return. There is no separately confirmed standard Crownwing refund-processing timeframe.

Unless another method is lawfully agreed or permitted, reimbursement uses the original payment method. A refund-processing fee will not be charged where the law prohibits it. Refund eligibility and timing must not be replaced by an unsupported blanket no-refunds statement.

Tell us promptly if you believe the wrong bird was supplied, the bird does not match the agreed description, documentation is missing or another significant delivery or contractual concern has arisen. Provide the order or invoice reference, date of handover and a clear explanation. Relevant photographs, video or veterinary information may assist an assessment.

Available remedies depend on the facts and applicable law. Crownwing Parrots will consider concerns in accordance with contractual and statutory rights, rather than treating every concern as a voluntary return. For an urgent health or welfare issue, contact an appropriate veterinary professional; website correspondence is not emergency veterinary care.

Request changes to the selected bird, delivery address, date or other details as early as possible. A change is subject to availability, suitable transport and documentation. Any resulting price change or extra cost must be explained before the change is agreed; a customer request does not itself confirm a revised reservation.

Sales and any transport must meet the animal-welfare, licensing, wildlife and import or export requirements applicable to the particular activity, species and destination. Where a permit, certificate or other document is required, it must be dealt with before the relevant handover.

This policy is not a claim that Crownwing holds a particular licence, certification or international transport authorisation. Ask for the actual records relevant to your proposed purchase; do not infer approval from a general policy page or a species guide.

Before paying, obtain the bird’s identity and price; accepted payment instructions; any deposit amount and refund conditions; the proposed collection or delivery location and costs; estimated dates; applicable cancellation rights; any additional voluntary return terms; and the refund arrangements. Keep the quotation and agreement for your records.

These are transaction-specific terms, not hidden fixed conditions. The business has not yet set standard figures for deposits, delivery charges, cancellation fees, voluntary-return windows or refund-processing time. If a term remains unclear, ask for written clarification before proceeding.

Send a complaint to info@crownwingparrots.co.uk or crownwingparrots@gmail.com with your contact details, relevant reference and the outcome you are seeking. Include supporting information where helpful, but do not send unnecessary sensitive documents. The business can use this information to investigate and respond.

Policy changes should be clearly dated. They do not retrospectively replace the terms of an existing agreement or remove non-excludable consumer rights. General website information is not a substitute for the specific disclosures required before an individual sale.

A clear explanation of browser storage and external services used by the current Crownwing Parrots website.
Last updated: 2 October 2026

Cookies are small pieces of information stored by a browser for a website. Similar technologies include local storage and session storage. These can support necessary functions or optional activities such as measuring visits and advertising.

The current site’s own code does not set cookies or store enquiry details in local storage or session storage. It does not contain Google Analytics, advertising pixels, a newsletter tracker or a shopping basket. Browsing and downloading an enquiry do not require accepting optional tracking.

The hosting or preview environment may have its own infrastructure behaviour. This statement describes the Crownwing website code, not a guarantee that every browser, hosting platform, email provider or external site uses no cookies.

Our styles request fonts from fonts.googleapis.com and fonts.gstatic.com. Google states that the Google Fonts API does not set or log cookies. It does receive technical request information, including an IP address, requested URL and HTTP headers that can include browser and referrer information.

No advertising-consent banner is displayed merely to suggest that the site uses tracking when it does not. The absence of cookies does not mean a font request is anonymous; the Privacy Policy explains the related information disclosure.

A prepared enquiry is a text file downloaded to your device, not a cookie. This website does not retain the entered details after the page is discarded or send them to the business. Your browser’s own autofill, download history and caching features are controlled by your browser settings.

You can inspect or remove cookies and website storage using your browser’s privacy settings. You can also clear autofill and downloaded enquiry files separately. Blocking external font requests may change the typeface shown but does not prevent you from reading the policy text.

Following a link to another website, or sending an email through your chosen provider, takes you to services with their own privacy and cookie arrangements. Review their notices if you want to understand those services.

Any future non-essential cookies or similar tracking will need an updated notice and, where legally required, a way to give or refuse consent before that tracking starts. Such a feature is not included in the current website. Contact us if you have questions about what this site loads.

THE CROWNWING CARE LIBRARY
Use specific questions to understand the individual bird and the proposed purchase before agreeing to a handover.

Ask for the exact species, known age and any identifying information. Find out how long the bird has been with its current keeper and what is known about its earlier history. Do not assume “young”, “baby” or “hand-reared” tells you everything needed to make a decision.

Ask which details are supported by records. If some information is unknown, have that stated clearly. Request any documentation relevant to the particular species and transaction, and confirm requirements with the appropriate official source where needed.

Request a description of the actual daily feeding routine, including foods the bird reliably eats. Ask about known health issues, previous veterinary examinations and available records. Agree how existing information will be passed on.
Discuss exercise, sleeping arrangements, cleaning and enrichment. These details help you prepare a stable transition rather than replacing every part of the bird’s routine immediately.

Ask how the individual reacts to familiar and unfamiliar people, how it communicates discomfort and what kinds of interaction it prefers. If you have children, pets or existing birds, discuss those circumstances before choosing.
Look for context rather than absolute promises. Talking, tameness and sociability vary. A bird that steps onto one person’s hand may still need patience and gradual training with another.

Confirm the specific bird, price, what is included, any proposed deposit and the applicable terms. Verify the person or business you are dealing with and the arrangements for viewing and handover. Ask questions before transferring money.
Discuss collection or delivery rather than assuming either service is offered. Confirm the care information and records that will accompany the bird. Keep a copy of what has been agreed.

Work through home and first-week preparation and identify an avian vet. Check the enclosure, food, safe perches and transport arrangements ahead of time. If you already keep birds, obtain professional advice on separation and health precautions.
Use Crownwing’s UK buying enquiry pages to explore a particular group, then prepare an enquiry with the questions you still need answered.

A practical starting point for comparing species, routines, noise, space and long-term care.

Write down what an ordinary week looks like, including work, travel and time away from home. Identify who will provide feeding, cleaning, enrichment and interaction. A sustainable routine should work beyond weekends and the first few weeks.

Then consider the household. Noise tolerance, usable space, other animals and the expectations of everyone living with the bird can change which species are appropriate. Make these decisions before narrowing the shortlist.

Group names are helpful for browsing, but they do not describe identical needs. Small and large macaws differ substantially; parakeets include birds with very different adult sizes and lifespans. Use the parrot collection to explore groups, then ask about the exact species.

Compare diet, accommodation, vocalisation and long-term commitment together. A smaller bird is not automatically a quiet or low-maintenance bird, and talking ability should not be treated as an essential feature.

Ask what the bird enjoys, what makes it uncomfortable and how it reacts to unfamiliar people. Request an explanation of its current routine and the information available about its history. Ask for recent photographs or video and distinguish documented facts from assumptions.
Behaviour is influenced by environment and experience. A label such as “friendly” cannot guarantee that a bird will immediately behave the same way in your home. Allow room for gradual adjustment.

Select two or three possibilities and compare the real daily requirements. Consider what would happen if your working hours changed or you needed someone else to care for the bird. Review ongoing ownership costs as well as purchase price.

Before making a commitment, work through the buying checklist and home preparation guide . A sensible match should remain practical even when the bird is vocal, independent or uninterested in talking.
THE CROWNWING CARE LIBRARY
Understand the feeding questions to discuss before choosing food or changing your bird’s routine.

Ask for the current feeding routine, not only a list of foods that have been offered. A bird may select favourite items from a mixed bowl and leave the rest. Record the foods, quantities and preparation methods before considering changes.
Feeding advice should reflect the exact species, age, health and activity level. Our species guides introduce the groups, but an individual plan belongs in a conversation with an avian vet.

The RSPCA recommends suitable complete pellets alongside varied fresh vegetables and fruit for many parrots. Species with different feeding needs require a tailored approach. An all-seed menu can be nutritionally unbalanced.

Offer clean water and maintain hygienic feeding equipment. Fresh foods need appropriate handling and removal when spoiled. Food selection should support a workable everyday routine rather than depend on occasional elaborate meals.
Use seeds and nuts thoughtfully as part of the bird’s overall intake rather than letting rewards replace balanced food. Discuss portion sizes and any supplements with an avian vet.

Dietary conversion should be planned carefully. Do not simply remove familiar food and assume the bird will eat its replacement. Ask for guidance on monitoring intake and body condition during a change.

Avocado is poisonous to parrots and must not be offered. Check unfamiliar foods with a trusted bird-care source before sharing them. Keep food preparation separate from household items or substances that may be hazardous to birds.
For further guidance, read the RSPCA parrot feeding advice . Return to the care hub for housing, enrichment and home preparation.
THE CROWNWING CARE LIBRARY
Plan accommodation, safe exercise and daily activities around the individual bird.

Start with the exact species and adult size. The enclosure must suit the bird’s movement and provide safe spacing between bars. Think about internal layout: food bowls and toys should not fill all the room available for movement.
Consider where the enclosure will stand, how it will be cleaned and whether the household can offer safe exercise outside it. A beautiful cage is not enough if the practical routine does not work.

Prepare an area for supervised activity with doors and windows secured and household hazards addressed. Think through interactions with people, pets and other birds. Choose arrangements that can be followed consistently.
Do not assume all parrots can share an enclosure. Ask for advice on species-appropriate social arrangements and careful introductions. The RSPCA housing guidance offers a useful starting point.
Provide appropriate opportunities to explore, chew, climb and search for food. Choose toys for the individual’s size and beak strength, inspect them regularly and remove damaged or unsafe items.

Introduce new activities thoughtfully and observe how the bird responds. Enrichment should support normal behaviour, not simply make the enclosure look busy. See the RSPCA enrichment guidance for ideas.
Make cleaning, equipment checks and replacement of damaged items part of the routine. Prepare the room as well as the enclosure; safe housing depends on the whole environment.
Use the preparation checklist to review household hazards, and the ownership cost guide to allow for equipment and ongoing replacement.
THE CROWNWING CARE LIBRARY
Build a realistic budget for accommodation, everyday care and the unexpected.

The initial price of a parrot is only one part of ownership. Start by identifying the exact species and suitable equipment rather than comparing birds on price alone. A smaller bird still needs an appropriate environment and veterinary care.
Request a clear price for the specific individual and an explanation of what is included. Our UK buying enquiry hub explains the information to confirm before proceeding.

Allow for accommodation, appropriate perches, feeding equipment, transport and safe enrichment. Large parrots may require robust equipment and more usable space. Assess the actual products and arrangements needed for your chosen species.
Do not buy an enclosure solely because it is advertised for parrots. Check size, usable layout, bar spacing and suitability with an informed source. See the housing guide before finalising the setup.

Budget for food, cleaning supplies, replacement toys and worn equipment. Plan for routine veterinary care and ask local avian practices about their services and costs. Prices vary by location, provider and the bird’s needs, so obtain relevant quotations.
Also consider care when you travel or cannot follow the usual routine. Identify suitable help and establish its availability rather than treating it as an afterthought.

Unexpected health concerns and changes in household circumstances can affect costs. Keep a practical reserve and think about long-term arrangements, particularly for birds that may be companions for decades.
Money is only part of the commitment. Daily time and consistency matter too. Use the species selection guide to check whether the financial and practical requirements fit your home.
THE CROWNWING CARE LIBRARY
Prepare the space, understand the existing routine and leave room for a gradual adjustment.

Have suitable accommodation, food, clean water, safe perches and appropriate enrichment ready before bringing the bird home. Check the layout and make sure the care arrangements are understood by everyone involved.

Ask for the individual bird’s established diet, daily routine and handling preferences. Keep this information accessible so the transition does not depend on remembering a brief conversation at handover.

Birds can be vulnerable to airborne hazards. Review cookware, aerosols, smoke and other products used around the home. Avoid exposing birds to PTFE-coated cookware fumes, and choose an appropriate location away from household hazards.
Secure windows, doors and electrical cords. Manage interactions with other animals carefully. Consult VCA’s household hazard guidance and ask your avian vet about your particular setup.

Identify an avian vet before the bird arrives and establish how to obtain urgent advice if needed. Ask what records to bring and discuss initial assessment, feeding and any precautions around existing birds.
Health questions are easier to manage with a clear contact and a record of the bird’s background. Do not wait until a concern arises to start searching for appropriate veterinary help.

Give the bird time to observe its new surroundings. Avoid expecting immediate handling, speech or affection. Watch how it responds and follow a steady routine informed by the information you received.
Maintain familiar food while discussing changes with an avian vet. Read the diet guide and housing guide before making major changes.

UK LOCATION GUIDES

Belfast is in Northern Ireland. If a parrot enquiry could involve movement between places, identify both the bird’s origin and intended destination early; proposed arrangements and any applicable requirements need careful, individual confirmation.

In an initial discussion, explain where the bird would currently be located if known and where it would be going. Do not infer the route, handover point or feasibility from a city name or from what may have happened in another enquiry.

Ask which details are confirmed for this individual and which remain undecided. Keeping origin and destination explicit helps identify the right questions before anyone makes a commitment or travel plan.

If any proposed movement raises questions about documentation or other requirements, consult the appropriate official sources for the actual origin, destination and circumstances. This guide does not make a legal determination or establish that any particular movement is permitted.

Ask the people involved what records are available, then verify requirements independently before proceeding. Do not assume that general information or a previous transaction settles the details of a different bird or route.

Research the exact species’ accommodation, social needs, diet and activity independently of travel discussions. African Grey Parrots, Amazons and small psittacines have differing requirements, and a broad category is not enough to choose equipment.

Plan an enclosure, supervised exercise, daily care and appropriate veterinary support. Doing this research early helps you decide whether the bird could suit your household even if an arrangement cannot be confirmed.

Request the exact species, known age, established diet, history and available records. Ask what is known about the bird’s routine and how it responds to handling or new people, and distinguish observation from unverified assumptions.

If images are shared, make sure they relate to the individual being discussed. Ask what care notes could accompany a transition and what questions should be resolved before any proposal is considered.

Decide who will provide daily care and who could help during an absence. Include food preparation, cleaning, enrichment and quiet time, and make sure any backup person understands the bird’s routine and boundaries.

Consider how a journey, if eventually agreed, could affect the bird’s transition. Prepare a calm arrival space and keep familiar information available, while avoiding assumptions about timing or transport until confirmed.

This page does not promise a Belfast branch, local availability, collection option or transport service. Ask directly whether a specific viewing or handover can be proposed, and confirm all practical details with the people responsible.

Do not travel or make a purchase decision until origin, destination, responsibilities and any relevant official checks have been addressed. The city form only creates a downloadable copy for your own preparation; it does not send a message.
UK LOCATION GUIDES

Birmingham is in the West Midlands, with households and living arrangements that differ from one another. Before considering a bird, bring everyone affected into the conversation and test whether the daily responsibilities and environment work for the household as a whole.

List the concerns each person has about sound, cleaning, time and interaction. A parrot changes the shared home even when one adult takes primary responsibility, so agreement should cover ordinary care as well as the excitement of bringing a bird home.

Consider children, visitors and other animals without assuming that a bird will welcome contact. Establish adult supervision, secure boundaries and quiet opportunities for the bird to move away from attention.

African Grey Parrots, Amazons and small psittacines each cover a range of birds and needs. Compare the exact species for vocal behaviour, social interaction, enrichment and likely adult size instead of using a broad category as a personality prediction.

Ask what is known about the particular bird’s responses to handling, new surroundings and different people. A description such as confident or friendly needs context and does not guarantee how the bird will behave with every member of a household.

Name the person responsible for routine tasks and decide how everyone else can help. Set up a simple way to share information about food, cleaning and observed preferences so changes in household availability do not leave basic care uncertain.

Make sure the main carer has time for species-appropriate exercise and interaction. If care is shared, each person should understand the bird’s boundaries and avoid forcing handling to create a quick bond.

Review where an enclosure can stand without blocking household movement and how the bird could have supervised time outside it. Check doors, windows, cooking areas and access by other pets as part of the room plan.
Equipment should fit the exact bird’s size and beak strength. Ask what the individual currently uses and what familiar items, food or routines may help make a move less confusing.

Ask for the exact species, known age, current diet, background and available records. Clarify what is known about social experience, vocal habits and handling preferences, and request recent information about the actual bird rather than relying on a generic species image.
Explain who lives in the home, what experience is present and how care would be shared. Ask what further preparation is recommended and what terms or arrangements would need separate confirmation.

No local viewing, collection point or transport arrangement is established by reading this guide. If an enquiry concerns a specific bird, ask directly whether a handover option can be agreed and who would be responsible for its details.

Only plan travel after the location, timing and appropriate carrier have been discussed and confirmed. Keep a written record of what has been agreed and make sure the bird’s routine and welfare remain central.
UK LOCATION GUIDES

Bristol is in South West England, but a bird’s suitability is determined by its needs and the home you can prepare. Start by making a safe exercise plan and choosing equipment for an exact species, rather than for an imagined ideal room.

Walk through the intended space from a bird’s perspective: check windows and doors, electrical leads, fans, cooking surfaces and access to unsuitable foods or other animals. Work out how the room can be secured each time the bird is out.

Decide where the bird can climb, perch and explore safely, and where it can rest without continual disturbance. Your plan should suit the household’s actual layout rather than rely on a room being used only occasionally.

Caiques are energetic and inquisitive; conures range in size and vocal character; cockatoos have strong social needs. Compare these differences in daily care and noise instead of selecting by colour or by one appealing behaviour.

Ask about adult size, enrichment and the individual’s experience with exercise. A smaller bird still needs a stimulating environment, while large equipment must be accommodated in a practical and safe way.

Select perches, toys and foraging opportunities for the species and the individual’s size and beak. Observe what is used, inspect equipment regularly and remove items that are damaged or unsuitable rather than assuming a large collection equals good enrichment.

Ask what activities the bird already knows and introduce unfamiliar options gradually. Include time for observation in the routine: a bird’s response can help you adjust the environment without pressuring it to engage.

Decide who will supervise exercise and how other household members will keep doors and other animals under control. Consistent steps reduce the chance that an otherwise safe space becomes risky when someone is in a hurry.
Include cleaning, food preparation, interaction and quiet rest in a normal day. Identify backup care and explain the routine clearly to anyone who might help when your plans change.

Confirm exact species and known age, then ask about current diet, history, handling preferences and the information or records available. Ask what has been observed about exercise and how the bird responds to unfamiliar surroundings.
Share your proposed room and care schedule. Request current images or other relevant details of the individual and clarify anything you would need to prepare before a possible transition.

A Bristol guide does not establish a local service, viewing arrangement or collection option. Ask directly whether anything can be arranged for the specific bird and confirm the location and responsibilities before making travel plans.
If a handover is agreed, discuss timing and suitable transport equipment with the relevant people. Make sure there is a plan for keeping the bird secure and limiting disruption during the journey.
UK LOCATION GUIDES

Cardiff is in South Wales. A helpful shortlist begins with your home, available time and tolerance for natural bird sounds, then compares exact species against those conditions rather than relying on appearance or broad category names.

Write down the space available, who lives in the home and how much daily time can be set aside for care. Consider how natural calls would fit your household and neighbours, without assuming a species will remain quiet.
Choose a few groups to research in depth rather than starting with a favourite colour. Compare social needs, activity, likely adult size, diet and lifespan as parts of the same decision.

African Grey Parrots include Congo and Timneh species; parakeets and small psittacines are an even wider grouping. Conures differ from one another too. Each label is a starting point for research, not a guarantee of temperament or suitability.

Identify the exact species before choosing an enclosure, food or companion plan. Ask about individual traits separately from general species information, especially where the bird’s history is incomplete.

Discuss cleaning, supervised exercise, visitor boundaries and who provides care when the main carer is unavailable. If other pets or young children are present, plan how the bird can be protected from unwanted contact.

Think about how a new parrot would fit into ordinary routines, not only the first weeks. The household should be comfortable supporting the bird even if it does not talk or enjoy the handling someone expected.

Request the exact identity, known age, current diet, history and records available. Ask which behaviours have been observed directly, including response to handling, unfamiliar people and the ordinary sounds of the home.
Explain the care plan you can offer and ask what additional information might help assess a match. Availability by itself does not show that a particular bird suits your household.

Set up suitable accommodation, identify appropriate veterinary support and plan enrichment before a possible arrival. If you already keep birds, research separation and seek suitable advice before considering introductions.

Keep a list of unanswered questions about terms, records and the bird’s routine. Take time to review the information against the needs of the species instead of treating an initial conversation as a decision deadline.

This South Wales guide does not establish local collection, viewing or transport availability. If a specific enquiry progresses, ask directly whether an arrangement can be agreed and confirm its location before you make plans.

Discuss responsibilities, timing and a suitable carrier before any journey. Prepare to maintain the bird’s established routine as far as practical, and only act on details that have been confirmed for the individual.
UK LOCATION GUIDES

Edinburgh lies in east central Scotland. A parrot decision is best tested against more than the life you have this month: consider how you could sustain care through changes in work, household, accommodation or the people who help you.

Consider possible changes to work patterns, household membership and accommodation. Ask whether you could still provide suitable space and daily interaction if your routine became busier or a regular carer moved away.
Species differ in lifespan and care needs, so research the exact bird rather than applying one broad expectation to all parrots. Discuss known age and background as part of any individual enquiry.

Identify someone who could realistically help if you were unavailable, and consider how they would learn the bird’s food, routine and boundaries. A name on a plan is not enough unless the person understands the commitment and agrees to the role.
Keep care notes accessible and update them when the routine changes. Include emergency contacts and information about suitable veterinary support so that another carer is not left to guess.

Cockatoos can have intensive social needs, African Grey Parrots benefit from thoughtful mental engagement and Eclectus care includes particular questions about established nutrition. Their needs should be researched separately rather than compressed into a single idea of parrot ownership.
Read about routine, enrichment, vocalisation and housing alongside expected lifespan. Consider whether the full pattern of care can fit your future plans, not only the appeal of a bird now.

Think beyond a purchase to food, replacement equipment, enrichment and veterinary care. Ask relevant providers about costs for your circumstances and include a reserve for changes rather than relying on an unverified general figure.
Consider who will meet the bird’s needs during holidays or other absences. Include the cost and practical availability of backup care in the wider plan before moving forward.

Ask about the individual’s age, history, established diet, social routine and any available records. Find out what care information would be provided and which details are uncertain, especially where future routine depends on a known preference.
Share how you would handle absence or a change in your own circumstances. Ask whether the bird’s known needs appear compatible with that plan, without treating a brief description as a guarantee.

Native to Australia, budgies are naturally social and active. They use flight, calls and close observation to interact with their surroundings. Captive birds need room to move, opportunities to forage and a safe social environment; their small size does not make companionship optional.

Budgerigars are often curious, alert and communicative. Individuals may be more comfortable with people, other budgies or a mixture of social experiences. Allow a new bird time to settle and build trust gradually; chasing or grabbing can make handling frightening rather than familiar.

As flock-oriented birds, they need meaningful social contact. If kept alone, they require regular interaction and enrichment from their people; if housed with another budgie, monitor compatibility and provide enough resources. A companion does not remove the need for daily observation and care.

A typical budgerigar measures about 18 cm from head to tail and often weighs around 30–40 g, although size varies with build and variety. A spacious enclosure should prioritise usable horizontal flight space, safe bar spacing and multiple perches rather than decorative clutter.

Many companion budgies live around 7–12 years, but an individual’s lifespan varies. Plan for care over years, including safe housing, companionship and access to an avian veterinarian. A small bird can still depend on its keeper every day.

Budgies often chatter, chirp and whistle throughout the day. Some learn to imitate words or sounds, but speech depends on the individual and is never guaranteed. Flock calls and lively conversation are normal behaviours, so consider whether their frequent vocal activity suits the home.

These intelligent small parrots can learn through patient, reward-based interaction. Offer target training, gentle step-up practice and simple foraging challenges. Speak softly, keep sessions short and stop if the bird appears uncomfortable. Learning is enrichment, not a test of whether the bird is tame or valuable.

Use a balanced species-appropriate diet, often based on suitable formulated food with a variety of fresh vegetables and some appropriate seed. Avoid relying entirely on a seed mix. Ask an avian veterinarian about the bird’s current diet, body condition and gradual transitions rather than following a one-size-fits-all ration.

Allow safe flight and movement in a bird-proofed space, with natural-looking perches, chewable materials and opportunities to search for food. Check bar spacing and toys carefully; small birds can become entangled in loose fibres or unsafe attachments. Keep the enclosure clean and provide undisturbed rest.

Budgerigars can suit a range of households willing to provide daily care, but they are not disposable starter pets. Their social needs, noise and sensitivity deserve respect. Children should learn calm observation and interact only with an adult supervising, while the bird has somewhere quiet to retreat.

Ask about the bird’s age, diet, social history and comfort with handling. Consider whether you can provide a companion or regular interaction, safe flight space and ongoing care. Confirm individual availability directly; this guide does not imply a budgerigar is currently in stock.

The Indian Ringneck is a long-tailed, medium-sized parakeet known for its alert nature and potential to learn sounds. It needs patient socialisation, regular flight and enrichment, and should not be chosen on assumptions about speech or tameness.

Indian Ringnecks have a slender body, long pointed tail and strong red bill. Green is common in the wild-type form, and captive colour varieties are widely seen. Adult males typically develop a dark and rose-coloured neck ring; females and young birds may not show the same markings. Colour varieties and age can make visual sex identification uncertain.

The species belongs to the rose-ringed parakeet group and is native across parts of Africa and South Asia. Its nimble flight and active exploratory behaviour mean a home needs safe movement space as well as an enclosure.

Indian Ringnecks are often observant and independent, with individual differences in confidence and willingness to handle. Some go through periods of greater wariness as they mature. Patient, choice-based interaction is more helpful than assuming a bird should always accept hands or close contact.

They need daily social interaction and things to do when people are busy. A predictable routine, training and foraging can help structure time. Respect boundaries and let the bird retreat; children should never handle a parakeet without close adult supervision.

An Indian Ringneck measures around 40 cm from head to tail, with the long tail contributing much of its length, and commonly weighs about 110–140 g. Figures vary. Give it room to climb and exercise, appropriate bar spacing and safe opportunities for supervised flight in a prepared space.
A companion may live around 20–30 years, but lifespan depends on the individual and care. Include a long-term plan, ongoing care and potential future guardianship in your decision.

Ringnecks can produce loud calls and some individuals learn words or other sounds. Talking ability cannot be guaranteed, and frequent vocalisation may be challenging for neighbours. Consider sound levels and how much daily activity the bird will hear when the home is empty.

They are capable learners and can benefit from short reward-based sessions. Teach target following, voluntary step-up and carrier entry. Foraging and safe chew materials add independent mental activity. A bird that does not talk or accept handling is still a complete companion and should not be pressured to perform.

Offer suitable formulated food and varied fresh vegetables, with fruit and seed treats used thoughtfully. A seed-only diet is not an adequate default. Have an avian veterinarian review an individual bird’s existing food and body condition, and guide any transition or supplement decisions.

Choose a secure enclosure with ample usable space, varied perches and climbing opportunities. Safe out-of-cage exercise, foraging and chewable enrichment help meet activity needs. Inspect toys for damage and secure windows, mirrors, fans and doors before supervised flight.

An Indian Ringneck may suit a patient household that accepts an active, independent bird and can provide exercise, enrichment and long-term daily care. It may not suit someone expecting a cuddly, immediately tame or reliably talking pet. Families should manage interactions calmly and consistently.

Ask about age, current diet, handling history, training and individual response to household activity. Prepare flight space and think through care over decades. Ask whether this particular bird is available now; a species guide is not an availability listing.

The Peach-faced Lovebird is a small, compact African parrot with a peach-coloured face and lively, confident manner. It needs companionship, flight and engaging activity, while its strong personality calls for respectful handling and planning.

Peach-faced Lovebirds have a green body, peach-pink face and chest, and a short, rounded tail. Captive colour mutations can produce other combinations, but the species is identified by its compact form and characteristic face in the wild-type bird. It is native to south-western Africa.

Despite their small size, lovebirds are active parrots with strong bills and clear preferences. They need more than a tiny cage and a mirror: safe flight, social contact and opportunities to forage and chew are central to daily life.

Peach-faced Lovebirds are often energetic and bold, but handling style and sociability vary from bird to bird. Some are content to observe before approaching; others are more interactive. Slow trust-building and respect for signals make safer interactions than grabbing or persistent handling.

The common name does not mean a bird must live as a bonded pair, nor does keeping two guarantee companionship without conflict. Social arrangements require thought, observation and enough resources. A single bird needs meaningful daily interaction, while compatible birds still need individual attention and monitoring.

Adults are generally around 15–18 cm long and weigh roughly 40–60 g. Their short proportions conceal a lively temperament. Enclosure bar spacing must prevent escape or injury, while providing enough room for movement, climbing and multiple perches. Daily supervised exercise in a secure area is valuable.

Many companion Peach-faced Lovebirds live around 10–15 years, and some may live longer; no single figure predicts an individual. Plan for long-term care, suitable companionship, routine observation and access to an avian veterinarian.

Lovebirds can be surprisingly loud for their size, with sharp calls and persistent chatter. Individual sound levels vary, but they should not be selected as a quiet alternative to larger parrots. Speech is not a typical guarantee; any learned sounds depend on the individual.

Short, positive-reinforcement sessions can build cooperation around stepping onto a perch, returning to the enclosure and entering a carrier. Offer simple foraging and safe objects to explore. Teach children calm observation and do not encourage biting or rough play as entertainment.

A balanced diet should include appropriate formulated food and a varied selection of fresh vegetables, with seeds and fruit offered thoughtfully. Seed-only mixes are not a balanced plan. An avian veterinarian can discuss the individual’s existing food, body condition and gradual changes; supplements should not be given routinely without advice.

Provide secure, appropriately spaced bars, varied perches, safe shredding materials and supervised activity outside the cage. Rotate enrichment to maintain interest, and inspect cords and small attachments for hazards. Give the bird quiet rest as well as active play.

A Peach-faced Lovebird can suit people prepared for an alert, lively small parrot and willing to offer daily attention. It is not a hands-off decoration or automatically an easy pet for a child. Adults remain responsible for care, safe handling and any decisions about pairing or introductions.

Ask about age, diet, social history, handling and the bird’s routine. Think about safe exercise, companionship and long-term care. Confirm the availability of an individual bird directly; this page does not indicate that a Peach-faced Lovebird is in stock.
